objective.statement: Name and write intervals above the tonic, by number, in the Grade 2 major and minor keys.
successCriteria: I know to count both notes, so the tonic itself is 1.
I can number an interval above the tonic in A, B♭ or E♭ major.
I can do the same in A, E or D minor.

explanation.text: An interval is the distance between two notes. For now we give it a number only: count the letter names from the lower note to the upper note, counting both.

music.textAlternative: The notes of A major numbered 1 to 8 above the tonic A.

explanation.caption: Above the tonic A: B is a 2nd, C♯ a 3rd, D a 4th, E a 5th, F♯ a 6th, G♯ a 7th, and A an octave (8th).

explanation.text: The key tells you which sharps and flats are in the scale, so you use the key to write the note: a 3rd above A in A major is C♯, because C♯ is in the key.
In a minor key the same counting works. A 3rd above A in A minor is C; a 5th above D in D minor is A.
Count the letters, include both notes, and use the sharps and flats of the key.

music.textAlternative: Three treble notes: E flat, G and B flat.

steps: The tonic is E♭: that is 1.
Counting up two more letters, F and then G: G is the 3rd above E♭.
Two more: A♭, then B♭. B♭ is the 5th above E♭.
demonstration.textAlternative: In E flat major, G is a 3rd above the tonic and B flat is a 5th above it.

guided.prompt: In E minor, which note is a 4th above the tonic?

G.reason: G is a 3rd above the tonic. Count the tonic itself as 1 when you count up.

B.reason: B is a 5th above the tonic. Count the tonic itself as 1 when you count up.

hints: Count the tonic as 1 and go up the scale one letter at a time until you reach the number.

mistakes.counted-one-end-only: Count both notes: the bottom note is 1, then every letter name up to and including the top note.
mistakes.quality-from-wrong-key: Judge the quality by imagining the major scale on the lower note. Is the top note in it?
mistakes.compound-arithmetic: An octave plus a 5th is a 12th, not a 13th: the shared note is counted only once.
mistakes.enharmonic-spelling: That sounds right, but intervals depend on letter names. Check how many letter names the interval spans.
mistakes.augmented-diminished-swap: Is the interval a semitone bigger or smaller than the major/perfect version? Bigger means augmented; smaller means diminished (or minor).

feedback.fallback: Not quite. Count the letter names first, then compare with the major scale on the lower note.

recap: Count both notes when numbering an interval.
Use the key to know which sharps or flats are in the scale.
The same counting works in major and minor keys.

mastery.completion: The lesson is complete when every step has been answered correctly (retries allowed). Only first-attempt, hint-free independent answers count as mastery evidence; guided steps never do.
